summary: Examines randomized and changing MAC addresses. Long-lasting identifiers help track Internet users, and this informational document discusses the state of affairs on randomizing them to improve privacy, and the effects on networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Your device's hardware name tag can be used to follow you around. Devices now change the tag over time, and this explains what that does.

questions: how does mac randomization protect privacy
why do devices need randomized mac addresses
subtitle: Hiding device identities on wireless networks to protect user privacy and prevent tracking.

tldr.problem: Media Access Control (MAC) addresses are unique identifiers burned into network devices and broadcast over the air, making them easy targets for tracking users' movements and online activity.
tldr.mechanism: Devices can randomize or periodically change their MAC addresses, replacing permanent hardware identifiers with temporary locally-administered addresses that change by network, time period, or session.
tldr.outcome: Modern operating systems have adopted MAC randomization by default for Wi-Fi to reduce tracking, but this creates new challenges for network operators trying to identify and manage devices.

facts.label: Locally-administered bit
facts.value: 1 for locally assigned, 0 for globally unique

facts.label: Address duplication probability
facts.value: Negligible in networks of typical size

today: RFC 9724 is an Informational RFC that provides an overview of MAC address randomization activities across standards bodies as of March 2025. It has not been obsoleted and documents the current state of privacy mechanisms being developed by IEEE 802, IETF, and the Wireless Broadband Alliance.

sections.title: Privacy Threats from Permanent Identifiers
sections.content:
Internet users leave extensive digital footprints through cookies, social media activity, and communications logs. One persistent identifier that makes tracking particularly easy is the Media Access Control (MAC) address, a 48-bit hardware identifier present on every Ethernet and Wi-Fi interface. Unlike IP addresses that can change between networks, MAC addresses historically remained constant throughout a device's lifetime and were visible to anyone within radio range of a Wi-Fi network.

This permanence enabled a form of device tracking called link-layer tracking. An observer with a Wi-Fi receiver can passively listen to probe request frames sent by scanning devices (before they connect to any network) and record their MAC addresses. By collecting observations from multiple locations, tracking systems can map user movements across the city, identify home addresses, and correlate online activity with physical location.

Privacy concerns about permanent identifiers affect all protocol layers. IEEE 802 MAC addresses have historically been an especially easy target for such tracking, and several initiatives within standards bodies have emerged to address this vulnerability.
sections.plainLanguage: Your device's Wi-Fi hardware name tag never changes, and anyone nearby can see it. Bad actors can follow you around by watching for your specific name tag at different Wi-Fi networks.

sections.title: MAC Address Structure and Randomization
sections.content:
A standard 48-bit MAC address divides into two parts: the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI), the first three octets identifying the manufacturer, and the Network Interface Controller (NIC) Specific portion, the remaining three octets assigned by the manufacturer. One bit in the address indicates whether the address is universally administered (assigned by the manufacturer) or locally administered (set by the OS or administrator).

Randomization leverages the locally-administered bit. By setting this bit to 1, a device signals that the address is not globally unique, which means it can generate random values locally without coordinating with any global authority. This allows an OS to create random MAC addresses on demand without causing network collisions. Early experiments at IETF meetings (between November 2014 and March 2015) tested whether address duplication would be a problem and found the probability to be negligible, even with many devices randomizing simultaneously.

However, the experiments revealed a critical limitation: other protocol identifiers beyond the MAC address can reveal device identity. For example, a DHCP client identifier, if not also randomized, could still be used to track a device across networks. Effective privacy requires coordinating randomization across multiple protocol layers rather than addressing only the MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: The first part of the address identifies the manufacturer (Apple, Cisco, etc.). Devices can switch to using fake locally-made addresses instead of the real one. Using random addresses works fine in practice, but other parts of network protocols can still reveal who you are.

sections.title: Taxonomy of Randomization Strategies
sections.content:
Different approaches to MAC address randomization offer varying trade-offs between privacy and stability. The RFC defines six main strategies, each controlling when the device generates a new address. Per-Vendor OUI MAC (PVOM) is the traditional baseline: the manufacturer assigns a globally unique address at the factory and burns it into the device.

For randomized approaches, Per-Device Generated MAC (PDGM) randomly generates an address once at the device's first boot and stores it permanently. Per-Boot Generated MAC (PBGM) generates a new random address on every device startup, never persisting it. Per-Network Generated MAC (PNGM) generates a different address for each Wi-Fi network (identified by SSID) and remembers that mapping so the device uses the same random address each time it returns to that network.

Time-based strategies provide stronger privacy. Per-Period Generated MAC (PPGM) generates a new address periodically, typically every twelve hours, which requires the device to reconnect and obtain a new IP address through DHCP or IPv6 autoconfiguration. Per-Session Generated MAC (PSGM) generates a new address for each session (such as after logging in to a Wi-Fi portal or VPN), allowing seamless reconnection without disconnecting.
sections.plainLanguage: Devices can change their name tag in different ways: once ever, once per device restart, once per network, once per day, or once per login session. More frequent changes provide better privacy but may break some network services.

sections.title: Current Operating System Practices
sections.content:
By 2021, most modern operating systems implemented MAC address randomization by default for Wi-Fi, though using different strategies. Android 10 and later uses PNGM: it generates a randomized address per SSID and reuses that same address when reconnecting to the same network. If the device previously connected to a network with its real MAC address, it continues using the real address unless manually enabled for randomization. iOS 14 and later similarly uses PNGM, binding randomized addresses to the Basic SSID, but resets the address when the user forgets a Wi-Fi network.

Windows 10 implements PPGM with daily randomization and supports randomization for Wi-Fi scanning by default. Linux (Debian) offers more flexibility, supporting both PNGM and PSGM, with configurable per-SSID settings. Both iOS and Android randomize their MAC addresses during Wi-Fi scanning before associating to a network, making it harder to track devices through probe requests.

Starting with Android 12, the system began supporting non-persistent randomization in certain scenarios: when a network suggestion application requests it or for open networks without a captive portal. This stricter approach provides better privacy by ensuring a fresh address for each connection rather than reusing the same random address per network.
sections.plainLanguage: Apple and Google phones use a fake name tag for each Wi-Fi network and remember it. Windows changes the tag daily. Linux lets you customize when to change it. All modern phones now also use fake names when just scanning for networks.

sections.title: Standards Coordination and Privacy Challenges
sections.content:
IEEE 802 standards bodies have worked extensively on MAC randomization policy. Following a 2014 privacy tutorial at the IEEE 802 Plenary, the IEEE 802 Executive Committee created a Privacy Recommendation Study Group that produced multiple documents, including IEEE Std 802E (Recommended Practice for Privacy Considerations) and IEEE Std 802c (Local Medium Access Control Address Usage). These documents specify the Structured Local Address Plan (SLAP), which designates ranges of locally-administered addresses for different purposes: Standard Assigned Identifiers for use by IEEE standards and Administratively Assigned Identifiers for network administrators.

As of 2024, IEEE 802.11 has two task groups addressing MAC randomization: the 802.11bh task group mitigating effects on networks and services, and the 802.11bi task group defining new privacy mechanisms in the MAC specification. The Wireless Broadband Alliance has also documented use cases for Wi-Fi identification systems to remain viable despite widespread randomization.

The IETF has addressed related privacy issues in IPv6 address randomization (RFC 8981 and RFC 7217), which similarly randomize the Interface Identifier portion of IPv6 addresses to prevent device tracking at the network layer. A major conclusion from IEEE Std 802E is that defending privacy against sophisticated adversaries is difficult: individuals can be tracked by fingerprinting communication patterns beyond just MAC addresses or other permanent identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Network standards organizations (IEEE and IETF) are coordinating to balance privacy with the needs of networks and services. Even with fake MAC addresses, other parts of network traffic can still reveal who you are.
